newsitem.title: BELGIUM: ECOFIN approves French/German convergence plans.
newsitem.headline: ECOFIN approves French/German convergence plans.

text.p: European Union finance ministers on Monday approved the French and German economic convergence plan, aimed at bringing their economies into line for the start of European monetary union.
"They have aproved the (German) plan. There was only a short discussion," a delegation source said.
"The French plan has been approved," an EU source said.
Under the terms of its plan, Germany intends to cut its deficit to 2.9 percent of gross domestic product this year, down from 3.8 percent in 1996.

That would come in just below the strict target of three percent set in the Maastricht Treaty, which lays down the economic conditions countries must meet this year if they wish to join the single currency in 1999.
Unexpectedly high unemployment at the start of this year has led some independent economists to question whether this goal is achievable.
Germany and France are seen as essential founder members of the single currency.
All current indications suggest that French and German forecasts on economic convergence ahead of monetary union are "on the safe side", an EU source said on Monday.
"All the indications for the moment allow us to believe that their forecasts are on the safe side," the source said.
